newsitem.title: UK: TABLE TENNIS-CHINESE SET TO DOMINATE AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: TABLE TENNIS-CHINESE SET TO DOMINATE AGAIN.

text.p: It will need more
than acupuncture to cure the malaise affecting table tennis if
China complete a second successive clean sweep at the world
championships starting on Thursday.
China's plunder of all seven titles at the 1995 worlds in
Tianjin was on home territory but the Chinese were just as
dominating at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, winning all four gold
medals.
The sport faces a crisis as the Asian giants so monopolise
tournaments that it is becoming increasingly rare to see a
non-Chinese even make the semis.
And invariably when a semifinalist is not wearing a Chinese
shirt it turns out to be one of the vast red army of Chinese
exports who have found homes in other countries.
This syndrome has more impact on the women's game. Japan's
Asian champion Chire Koyama, who won the world title as He Zhili
in 1987, and Chen Jing - the 1988 Olympic champion as a Chinese
player and a silver medalist at Atlanta flying Taiwan colours -
continue to derail some of their old team mates, but only
occasionally.
Fans hoping to witness the great Chinese fall are likely to
be disappointed. Any wounds will be just like the pin pricks the
Chinese receive from their team acupuncturist. All their best
players will be on show and look as strong as ever.
In the men's event, defending champion Kong Kinghui's major
rival is compatriot Liu Guoliang, the hard-hitting 21-year-old
who conquered Kong in the Olympic final. Third seed Liu has set
his sights on competing the Grand Slam of Olympic, World Cup and
world championship titles, a feat achieved only by Sweden's
Jan-Ove Waldner.
Second seed Waldner, now 30, remains one of the leading
European hopes. A great all-rounder, Waldner has a good world
championship pedigree, having won the title in 1989 and been
runner-up twice in addition to helping Sweden to three team
triumps.
There are four other Europeans in the top 10 - the rapidly
improving Vladimir Samsonov of Belarus at number four, Belgium's
1993 losing finalist Jean-Michel Saive (8), Germany's Jorg
Rosskopf (9) and Croatian Zoran Primorac (10).
Sweden's 1991 world champion Jorgen Persson has dropped to
14th in the rankings, two places below Frenchman Jean-Philippe
Gatien, the 1993 title-holder.
The Chinese women look invincible. They have held the
singles title since 1979 and won the team title nine of the last
10 times.
Tiny world number one Deng Yaping seems to be in a class by
herself. After taking the world singles title for the first time
in 1991, she recaptured the crown four years later along with
the women's doubles.
Deng struck gold in the singles and doubles at the Atlanta
Olympics and then completed the grand slam by winning the World
Cup.
Significantly, China fill all but three of the top 10
women's standings and the only infiltrators are all former
Chinese stalwarts - Chen Jing (3), Koyama (8) and Hong Kong's
Chai Po-wa.
Players from 117 countries are competing in the championships
which end on May 5.
